snippet.title: Can 11 Meters Be Saved? The Future of CB Radio and Amateur Radio
snippet.description:
For decades, 11 meters (CB radio) has been viewed by many as a service in decline, while others continue to enjoy it every day for local communications, DX, antenna experimentation, and simply having fun on the air.

But what if the biggest problem with CB radio isn't the operators...

What if it's the way the service was designed?

In this video I take a thoughtful look at the history of Citizens Band radio, why it was placed in the HF spectrum, and whether it's time to rethink how 11 meters fits into today's radio landscape.

This is NOT a "CB vs Ham Radio" video.

Instead, I explore questions like:

Should 11 meters be modernized?
Would increasing the legal SSB power limit make sense?
Should modern export radios ever be legalized for compliant 11-meter operation?
Could better FCC enforcement improve the band?
Can CB radio and amateur radio work together instead of being viewed as rivals?
Could 11 meters once again become a gateway into amateur radio?

Along the way we'll discuss propagation, DX, the worldwide 11-meter community, club call signs, antennas, and why many hams—including me—first became interested in radio through CB.

Whether you're a CB operator, licensed amateur, or simply curious about radio communications, I'd love to hear your thoughts in the comments.

Videos Mentioned

► Salty Walt's original discussion that inspired part of this conversation:
https://youtu.be/tAwQqkPC91s?si=dbBHxVJZYdj84ivl

► HF Propagation Explained:
https://youtu.be/lIAasJC9D24?si=63qo3Y8__hjvreeX

► What is MURS? (Multi-Use Radio Service)
https://youtu.be/WyNjDFh9mdc?si=xQyetMjqWxmJipID

Questions for You

I'd love to hear your opinion.

Can 11 meters be saved?
Should the legal SSB power limit be increased?
Would 100 watts PEP be reasonable?
Should export radios be legalized if configured for compliant 11-meter operation?
Is better FCC enforcement the real answer?
Could organizations do more to promote good operating practices?
Can CB radio and amateur radio build stronger bridges between their communities?

Please keep the discussion respectful. There are good operators in both communities, and thoughtful conversations are how we all learn.

If you enjoyed this video, please consider giving it a 👍, subscribing, and sharing it with someone interested in radio communications.

For decades, 11 meters (CB radio) has been viewed by many as a service in decline, while others continue to enjoy it every day for local communications, DX, antenna experimentation, and simply having fun on the air.

But what if the biggest problem with CB radio isn't the operators...

What if it's the way the service was designed?

In this video I take a thoughtful look at the history of Citizens Band radio, why it was placed in the HF spectrum, and whether it's time to rethink how 11 meters fits into today's radio landscape.

This is NOT a "CB vs Ham Radio" video.

Instead, I explore questions like:

Should 11 meters be modernized?
Would increasing the legal SSB power limit make sense?
Should modern export radios ever be legalized for compliant 11-meter operation?
Could better FCC enforcement improve the band?
Can CB radio and amateur radio work together instead of being viewed as rivals?
Could 11 meters once again become a gateway into amateur radio?

Along the way we'll discuss propagation, DX, the worldwide 11-meter community, club call signs, antennas, and why many hams—including me—first became interested in radio through CB.

Whether you're a CB operator, licensed amateur, or simply curious about radio communications, I'd love to hear your thoughts in the comments.

Videos Mentioned

► Salty Walt's original discussion that inspired part of this conversation:
https://youtu.be/tAwQqkPC91s?si=dbBHxVJZYdj84ivl

► HF Propagation Explained:
https://youtu.be/lIAasJC9D24?si=63qo3Y8__hjvreeX

► What is MURS? (Multi-Use Radio Service)
https://youtu.be/WyNjDFh9mdc?si=xQyetMjqWxmJipID

Questions for You

I'd love to hear your opinion.

Can 11 meters be saved?
Should the legal SSB power limit be increased?
Would 100 watts PEP be reasonable?
Should export radios be legalized if configured for compliant 11-meter operation?
Is better FCC enforcement the real answer?
Could organizations do more to promote good operating practices?
Can CB radio and amateur radio build stronger bridges between their communities?

Please keep the discussion respectful. There are good operators in both communities, and thoughtful conversations are how we all learn.

If you enjoyed this video, please consider giving it a 👍, subscribing, and sharing it with someone interested in radio communications.

snippet.title: I Blamed the Antenna
snippet.description:
1 of 4. Große Schlicke, OE/TI-441, 2059 m.
Four contacts make a summit activation. I made one. It was not on the radio I carried up there for it.

We rode the cable car up with four kids and walked the ridge in the
Tannheimer Berge. The signs said one hour fifteen. I told the camera it
would take us two. It took us two. This is the highest our children have
ever climbed, and every part of that day ran exactly to schedule.

Then I put the antenna up and called CQ into nothing for twenty-seven
minutes.

Three things were wrong that day. I found two of them that evening in the tent, wrote them off, and went to sleep satisfied. The third one I did not find until months later, sitting in front of this footage - and it had been on my screen the whole time.

This is the whole day: the climb, the setup, the silence, and the post mortem. The one contact is logged, so the station who answered has their points. Thank you for coming back to me when nobody else did.

---
FOTA SOTA - Family On The Air. Six of us: two parents, four kids, one
station. We activate summits and parks together and we publish all of it, including the activations that do not work. New episode every Wednesday.

Honest activations. Real conditions. No reshoots.
---

STATION
Radio: Yaesu FT-857D
Antenna: EFHW with 49:1 transformer, inverted L on a fibreglass pole
Handheld: Baofeng, 2 m FM
Power: Enerblock 9 Ah LiFePO4
Modes: SSB and FM
Summit: OE/TI-441, Große Schlicke, 2059 m, Tannheimer Berge, Tirol
Callsign: OE/HF2LT/P
QSOs: 1

snippet.title: RFGEN44: Open USB 4.4 GHz RF Signal Generator
snippet.description:
RFGEN44 is a portable, fully open-source, USB-programmable RF signal generator covering 35 MHz to 4.4 GHz — your key to hassle-free RF signal generation.

https://www.crowdsupply.com/circuitvalley/rfgen44

If you work with RF, you need a signal source. Your options have always been limited: bench instruments that cost hundreds or thousands and lock you into one vendor's software. RFGEN44 sits between the throwaway modules and the expensive boxes — compact, driver-free over USB HID, cross-platform, and open at both the hardware and software level.

In this video:
00:00  What is the RFGEN44
00:35  Hardware tour — RF outputs, USB-C, AUX port, status LEDs
01:10  Plug-and-play + standalone operation (no PC required)
01:40  PCB and block diagram — MCU, ADF4351 PLL, AUX functions
02:10  Clean 100 MHz standalone signal on the spectrum analyzer
02:40  The open control software
03:10  Programming a frequency sweep (100–200 MHz)
03:40  Macro programming — sequences that run on the device
04:20  2 GHz sweep
04:45  10 kHz resolution on a Keysight 53220A frequency counter

FEATURES
- 35 MHz to 4.4 GHz output, 10 kHz step resolution
- Two complementary RF outputs (RF Out + / RF Out −), SMA
- Driver-free USB HID — works on Windows, Linux, and macOS with nothing to install
- On-device programmable macros — frequency, hold time, RF on/off — run standalone, looped, single-shot, or trigger-advanced
- AUX (Ref/Trigger) port: external reference in (10–250 MHz), internal reference out, sweep/macro sync out, sync in
- Internal 25 MHz ±50 ppm reference
- Standalone operation — outputs RF the moment you plug it in, no PC needed
- USB Type-C powered
- Fully open source — hardware and software
- Cross-platform Qt GUI + Python + raw HID (MATLAB, etc.)

The macro feature is especially useful for presence beacons, frequency hopping, and ham radio applications.

Built by Circuit Valley in Germany.

Full documentation, design files, and source code:
https://www.circuitvalley.com

snippet.description: This video breaks down why modernizing the Technician license is becoming one of the most important conversations in amateur radio. It traces the story from the stalled 2018 ARRL petition to the renewed 2025 push, showing how the rise of FT8, declining retention, evolving emergency‑comms needs, and the “VHF/UHF wall” have reshaped the landscape. The script argues that giving Technicians structured HF access isn’t lowering standards—it’s strengthening the hobby by increasing activity, improving training, boosting emergency readiness, and helping new operators experience the part of radio that keeps people hooked for life.

snippet.title: Beginner's Guide to Oscillators
snippet.description:
📡 Beginner’s Guide to Oscillators

How does a radio create a signal in the first place?

In this reel, we look at one of the most important building blocks in radio electronics — the oscillator.

⚡ An amplifier makes an existing signal larger.
〰️ An oscillator creates and maintains a repeating electrical waveform using energy from the power supply.

We cover:

🔹 What an oscillator actually does
🔹 Why feedback is needed
🔹 How oscillation can begin from tiny electrical noise
🔹 Sine waves versus square waves
🔹 How an LC circuit sets a resonant frequency
🔹 Why changing L or C changes frequency
🔹 What a VFO is — and why it can drift
🔹 Why quartz crystals provide much greater stability
🔹 How PLL frequency synthesis gives modern radios accurate, selectable frequencies
🔹 Why transmitters and receivers both need oscillators

In a transmitter, an oscillator can provide the RF carrier that is later modulated and amplified.

In a receiver, a local oscillator works with a mixer to convert an incoming signal to another frequency that is easier to filter, amplify and process.

Understanding oscillators is a major step towards understanding how a radio actually works. 📻

In this video, I take a closer look at the latest real-world photos of the Xiegu G7250, including the front control head and the rear of the RF unit, and dig into three specific hardware questions plus one increasingly important opinion: what should this radio actually cost?

First, the G7250 appears to have three different controls related to power. There is the prominent red power button on the control head, along with two rotary controls labeled with power-related functions. That raises an obvious question: which control manages which kind of power? Are we looking at radio power, transmit power, display power, or some combination of those functions?

Second, the rear of the G7250 reveals a pair of red and white RCA connectors. What exactly are they for? They could potentially be related to audio, I/Q, external accessories, or another function entirely. Until Xiegu releases complete documentation, the photographs give us clues but not the whole answer.

Third, we finally have a clear view of the G7250’s two SO-239 antenna connectors. That immediately raises another practical question: how do the dual antenna ports operate? Are they independently selectable by band, assigned separately to HF and 6 meters, switchable from the control head, or intended for another configuration?

The new rear-panel photos also show the large cooling fan, Anderson Powerpole-style DC input, accessory connector, DB9 connection, RJ45 network-style connector, chassis ground, and other details that give us our best look yet at how the G7250 RF deck is actually constructed.

Carine, HB9FZC und René, HB9NBG sind lizenzierte Funkamateure CEPT Class A. Als passionierte Berggänger erkunden die beiden seit über 20 Jahren die Schweizer Alpenwelt zu Fuss. Vor 10 Jahren haben sie das Bergfunk-Diplomprogramm SOTA für sich entdeckt und haben dadurch sowohl den Amateurfunkbetrieb als auch die Planung und Durchführung von Bergtouren von einer ganz neuen, sehr faszinierenden Seite kennengelernt. Als SOTA-Aktivatoren haben Carine und René schon viele Berggipfel entdeckt, von denen sie ohne SOTA wohl nie erfahren hätten, dass es sie gibt. Immer wieder ergeben sich dabei sportlich anspruchsvolle und ausgedehnte Bergtouren – im August 2026 zum Beispiel starten die beiden auf dem Grossen St.Bernhard Pass zu einem besonders beeindruckenden SOTA-Abenteuer mit der SOTA-Doppelaktivierung der Pointe de Drone auf 2’949m und dem Monts Telliers auf 2’951m… Lasst euch beeindrucken von unserem Erlebnisbericht! Carine, HB9FZC und René, HB9NBG sind lizenzierte Funkamateure CEPT Class A. Als passionierte Berggänger erkunden die beiden seit über 20 Jahren die Schweizer Alpenwelt zu Fuss. Vor 10 Jahren haben sie das Bergfunk-Diplomprogramm SOTA für sich entdeckt und haben dadurch sowohl den Amateurfunkbetrieb als auch die Planung und Durchführung von Bergtouren von einer ganz neuen, sehr faszinierenden Seite kennengelernt. Als SOTA-Aktivatoren haben Carine und René schon viele Berggipfel entdeckt, von denen sie ohne SOTA wohl nie erfahren hätten, dass es sie gibt. Immer wieder ergeben sich dabei sportlich anspruchsvolle und ausgedehnte Bergtouren – im August 2026 zum Beispiel starten die beiden auf dem Grossen St.Bernhard Pass zu einem besonders beeindruckenden SOTA-Abenteuer mit der SOTA-Doppelaktivierung der Pointe de Drone auf 2’949m und dem Monts Telliers auf 2’951m… Lasst euch beeindrucken von unserem Erlebnisbericht! snippet.title: «Regime de Vladimir Putin aproxima-se em determinadas alturas de místicos»
snippet.description:
«Regime de Vladimir Putin aproxima-se em determinadas alturas de místicos»

Esta quarta-feira no NOW, o Major-General Isidro de Morais Pereira analisou os potenciais impactos das perturbações ionosféricas e da alteração da luminosidade provocadas por um eclipse solar no contexto militar e geopolítico. O oficial explicou que o fenómeno causa uma transição rápida de luminosidade na ionosfera, afetando temporariamente as comunicações rádio de alta frequência (HF), ressalvando que "é algo temporário" e que "não afeta um conflito". Segundo o militar, este tipo de evento "pode ser essencialmente aproveitado para dissimular outro tipo de atividades", nomeadamente ciberataques ou testes de guerra eletrónica. Sobre o impacto no conflito europeu, afirmou que "não traria qualquer tipo de vantagem, nem para Ucrânia, nem para Federação Russa", destacando ainda que as forças militares tecnologicamente evoluídas contam com equipamentos de visão noturna e sistemas redundantes de posicionamento global (GPS) que minimizam perturbações. Abordou também o aproveitamento psicológico e de propaganda por regimes autoritários, sublinhando que a alteração no céu pode ser usada para construir uma "retórica imbatível" e manipular as populações perante o estresse de guerra.

snippet.title: What Ham Operators Heard The Night Nazis Invaded Poland
snippet.description:
On the night of August 31st, 1939, a transmission went out from a radio station near the German-Polish border. By the next morning, Adolf Hitler stood before the Reichstag declaring war, and within days, amateur radio licenses were being revoked across Europe. Germany's amateur community was shut down on the same morning as the invasion. Britain's followed within 72 hours.

But the shutdowns were only part of what happened. What followed for the operators themselves — in Germany, Britain, Poland, and the United States — involved classified intelligence work, confiscated equipment, and one story from occupied Poland that reaches far beyond amateur radio.

This is the full account of what ham operators heard, lost, and were conscripted to do when the Second World War began.

snippet.title: Hunting New POTA Parks Has Never Been This Easy! | ParkWatch
snippet.description:
Hunting Parks On The Air just got a whole lot easier.

In this video, I take you through the ParkWatch Hunting Page — the part of ParkWatch I probably use more than anything else.

Since launching ParkWatch to the amateur radio community, I have been averaging around 25 new POTA references every single day, and the Hunting Page is a big reason why.

ParkWatch was created because I wanted one amateur radio hunting tool that brought together the features I actually use.

Rather than jumping between spotting pages, logging programs, propagation tools and different applications, ParkWatch puts the information you need right in front of you.

And while Parks On The Air was a major reason I created ParkWatch, it certainly isn't limited to POTA.

ParkWatch also supports hunters chasing activity through programs such as:

• Parks On The Air — POTA
• World Wide Flora & Fauna — WWFF
• Lakes & Lagoons On The Air — LLOTA
• Islands On The Air — IOTA
• And more as ParkWatch continues to grow

Hunt The Way YOU Want

Not everyone hunts amateur radio the same way.

Maybe you're looking specifically for **new POTA references**.

Maybe you want to work everybody you can hear.

Maybe you're hunting CW, SSB, FT8 or another mode.

Maybe you're concentrating on a particular band, country, program or activator.

ParkWatch allows you to filter activity by **band, mode, program, needed parks, callsigns and many other criteria**, helping you quickly find the contacts that matter most to you.

Follow Your Friends

ParkWatch isn't just a spotting screen.

The ParkWatch Community features allow you to see what other ParkWatch users are hunting and discover what is generating activity across the community.

You can also watch for your friends and favourite operators, making it much easier to catch them when they appear on the air.

Track Your Progress

ParkWatch includes scorecard and statistics tools that help you follow your hunting progress day by day.

Watch those park totals climb.
Find new references.
Chase new countries.
Follow your goals.
And then start looking for the next one.

Check Current Band Conditions

Propagation is constantly changing.

ParkWatch puts current radio conditions alongside the activity you're already watching, helping you decide where to concentrate your hunting.

Instead of having multiple websites and applications open, more of the information you need is available in one place.

Why I Created ParkWatch

I built ParkWatch because I couldn't find one POTA hunting and portable amateur radio application that did everything I wanted.

There are some excellent tools available for amateur radio operators, but I continually found myself switching between different applications to get all the features I wanted.

So I decided to build my own.

ParkWatch is developed around the way I actually operate amateur radio, and it continues to evolve based on real-world use and feedback from other operators.

Best of all, ParkWatch is free for amateur radio operators.

👉 Try ParkWatch: parkwatch.online

If you're a POTA, WWFF, LLOTA or IOTA hunter — or you simply enjoy chasing interesting amateur radio activity — give ParkWatch a try and let me know what you think.

And if you enjoy portable amateur radio, DXing, antennas, experimentation and adventures from around Canada, make sure you **subscribe to Out N' Aboot With VE9CF**.
